'''''Vaccinium uliginosum''''' ('''bog bilberry''',<ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web |title=Bog Bilberry ''Vaccinium uliginosum'' L. |website=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.cy9 |access-date=2026-07-29}}</ref> '''bog blueberry''',<ref>{{PLANTS |id=VAUL |taxon=Vaccinium uliginosum |access-date=28 July 2015}}</ref> '''alpine blueberry''' or '''western blueberry''') is a Eurasian and North American [[flowering plant]] in the [[heath family]].<ref>{{Jepson eFlora|53312|Vaccinium uliginosum subsp. occidentale |first=Gary D. |last=Wallace |date=2017|access-date=18 July 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=''Vaccinium uliginosum'' — alpine blueberry|publisher=Native Plant Trust |date=2026 |access-date=17 January 2026|  url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/vaccinium/uliginosum/}}</ref> The berries are edible.

==Description==
''Vaccinium uliginosum'' is a small [[deciduous]] shrub growing to {{convert|10|-|75|cm|0}} tall, rarely {{convert|1|m|ft|abbr=off|0}} tall, with brown stems (unlike the green stems of the closely related [[Vaccinium myrtillus|bilberry]]). The [[leaves]] are oval, {{convert|4|-|30|mm|frac=8}} long and {{convert|2|-|15|mm|abbr=on|frac=16}} wide, blue-green with pale net-like veins, with a smooth margin and rounded apex.<ref name="Vander Kloet-2009">{{eFloras|1|family=Ericaceae|first=Sam P.|last=Vander Kloet}}</ref>

The [[flower]]s are pendulous, urn-shaped, pale pink, {{convert|4|–|6|mm|abbr=on|frac=16}} long, produced in mid-spring. The [[fruit]] is a dark blue-black [[berry (botany)|berry]] {{convert|5|-|8|mm|abbr=on|frac=32}} in diameter, with sweet white flesh, ripe in late summer.<ref name="Vander Kloet-2009"/> Cytology is 2n = 24.<ref name="Redpath-2022">{{cite journal | last1=Redpath | first1=Lauren E. | last2=Aryal | first2=Rishi | last3=Lynch | first3=Nathan | last4=Spencer | first4=Jessica A. | last5=Hulse-Kemp | first5=Amanda M. | last6=Ballington | first6=James R. | last7=Green | first7=Jaimie | last8=Bassil | first8=Nahla | last9=Hummer | first9=Kim | last10=Ranney | first10=Thomas | last11=Ashrafi | first11=Hamid | title=Nuclear DNA contents and ploidy levels of North American Vaccinium species and interspecific hybrids | journal=Scientia Horticulturae | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=297 | year=2022 | issn=0304-4238 | doi=10.1016/j.scienta.2022.110955 | article-number=110955| doi-access=free }}</ref> Its fruit [[persistence (botany)|persists]] for an average of 26.1 days, and bears an average of 24.7 seeds per fruit. The fruit averages 86.8% water, with the [[dry matter|dry weight]] including 38.4% [[carbohydrate]]s and 3.9% [[lipid]]s.{{sfn|Ehrlén|Eriksson|1991}}

== Subspecies ==
Three [[subspecies]] and one [[variety (botany)|variety]] are accepted by the [[Plants of the World Online]] (POWO) database,<ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=''Vaccinium uliginosum'' L. |website=Plants of the World Online |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30184367-2 |access-date=2026-07-29}}</ref> but not all authorities distinguish them. Only the nominate subspecies of ''V. uliginosum'' subsp. ''uliginosum'' is relatively widely accepted.<ref name="Vander Kloet-2009"/>

*''Vaccinium uliginosum'' var. ''japonicum'' <small>T.Yamaz.</small> — Japan
*''Vaccinium uliginosum'' subsp. ''nanum'' <small>(Boiss.) Rivas Mart., A.Asensi, Molero Mesa & F.Valle</small> — Spain (Sierra Nevada)
*''Vaccinium uliginosum'' subsp. ''uliginosum'' — throughout most of the range of the species
*''Vaccinium uliginosum'' subsp. ''vulcanorum'' <small>(Kom.) Alsos & Elven</small> — northeast Asia

A fourth subspecies ''Vaccinium uliginosum'' subsp. ''microphyllum'' <small>Lange</small> is sometimes accepted for Arctic plants; POWO treat it as a synonym of the nominate subspecies.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77224936-1 |title=''Vaccinium uliginosum'' subsp. ''uliginosum'' |publisher=Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |year=2023|access-date=8 November 2025}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
The plant is native to cool temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, at low altitudes in the [[Arctic]], [[Baltics]], and at high altitudes south to the [[Pyrenees]], the [[Alps]], and the [[Caucasus]] in Europe, the mountains of [[Mongolia]], northern [[China]], the [[Korean Peninsula]] and central [[Japan]] in Asia, and the [[Sierra Nevada (U.S.)|Sierra Nevada]] in [[California]] and the [[Rocky Mountains]] in [[Utah]] in North America.<ref name="Vander Kloet-2009" /><ref>{{eFloras|2|family=Ericaceae|last1=Fang|first1=Ruizheng<!-- This name seems to be given in the Chinese order, with surname first, as first names are more often two syllables and 方 (fāng) is listed as a surname on Wiktionary. -->|first2=Peter F.|last2=Steven}}</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=vaccinium+uliginosum Altervista Flora Italiana, Falso mirtillo, ''Vaccinium uliginosum'' L.]</ref><ref>{{BONAP|ref|genus=Vaccinium|species=uliginosum|state=1}}</ref>

It grows on wet [[acidic soils]] on [[heath]]land, [[moorland]], [[tundra]],<ref name="Turner-2014">{{Cite book |last1=Turner |first1=Mark |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VLbAAwAAQBAJ |title=Trees & Shrubs of the Pacific Northwest |last2=Kuhlmann |first2=Ellen |date=2014 |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |isbn=978-1-60469-263-1 |edition=1st |location=Portland, OR |pages=183}}</ref> and in the understory of [[conifer]]ous forests, from sea level in the Arctic, up to {{convert|3400|m|ft|abbr=on}} altitude in the south of the range. It is also occasionally found on calcareous soils on mountain ledges.<ref name="PlantAtlas"/>

''V. uliginosum'' can survive long, severe climatic oscillations.<ref name="Alexander-2017">{{cite journal |last1=Alexander |first1=Jake M. |last2=Chalmandrier |first2=Loïc |last3=Lenoir |first3=Jonathan |last4=Burgess |first4=Treena I. |last5=Essl |first5=Franz |last6=Haider |first6=Sylvia |last7=Kueffer |first7=Christoph |last8=McDougall |first8=Keith |last9=Milbau |first9=Ann |last10=Nuñez |first10=Martin A. |last11=Pauchard |first11=Aníbal |last12=Rabitsch |first12=Wolfgang |last13=Rew |first13=Lisa J. |last14=Sanders |first14=Nathan J. |last15=Pellissier |first15=Loïc |display-authors=3 |date=2017-11-27 |title=Lags in the response of mountain plant communities to climate change |journal=Global Change Biology |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=563–579 |doi=10.1111/gcb.13976 |issn=1354-1013 |pmc=5813787 |pmid=29112781}}</ref><ref name="De Witte-2011">{{cite journal |last1=De Witte |first1=LC |last2=Armbruster |first2=GFJ |last3=Gielly |first3=L |last4=Taberlet |first4=P |last5=Stocklin |first5=J |date=2011-11-10 |title=AFLP markers reveal high clonal diversity and extreme longevity in four key arctic-alpine species |journal=Molecular Ecology |volume=21 |issue=5 |pages=1081–1097 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-294x.2011.05326.x |issn=0962-1083 |pmid=22070158}}</ref>

== Uses ==
The berries can be eaten raw or cooked, used to make jelly or pies, or dried to make [[pemmican]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Nyerges|first=Christopher|title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods|publisher=Falcon Guides|year=2017|isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3|location=Guilford, CT|oclc=965922681}}</ref>

In [[Korean cuisine]], bog bilberry is used to make [[infused liquor]] (''Deuljjuk-[[Korean alcoholic drinks|sul]]'').
